text: Nicolaas Verkolje learned painting and engraving from his father Jan Verkolje in Delft, and his brother Jan II also became a painter. He specialized in history pieces and portraits in a classicistic style, and he also worked as a mezzotinter. He copied paintings by Antoine Coypel, Gérard de Lairesse, Godfried Schalcken, Gerard Dou, Adriaen van der Werff and Gabriel Metsu on commission and was influenced by them. At the beginning of the 18th century he went back to biblical and mythological themes and dynamic compositions.

Georges Michel was the son of an employee at Les Halles, and the support of a local tax farmer let him take lessons from a history painter named Leduc and enter the Académie de Saint-Luc, where he studied with Claude-Joseph Vernet. For years he lived meagrely as a drawing teacher. In 1789 he went to Germany with the Duke of Guiche and met Jean-Baptiste-Pierre Lebrun, who gave him a living restoring paintings and copying 17th-century Dutch landscapes. He first exhibited at the Salon in 1791 but apparently gained little recognition. His landscapes are considered a precursor of the Barbizon School.

Jan Nowopacký came from a poor family of weavers in Nechanice, and Countess von Harrach took him to Vienna to study with the portrait painter Franz Schrotzberg. The Academy of Fine Arts at first rejected him because he did not speak German well enough. He went home, studied hard, reapplied and was admitted in 1842. He made several study trips to the Alps and Tyrolia. In 1848 he took part in the Revolutions and returned to Prague when they failed. After his father's death he worked as a drawing teacher for the Paars family.

Johan Gørbitz was one of ten children of a successful merchant in Bergen. He studied at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in Copenhagen, worked as a portrait painter in Bergen and then traveled to Dresden and Vienna. In 1809 he moved to Paris, where he remained a popular portrait painter for many years. He returned to Norway in 1836 and settled in Christiania, where he painted many prominent Norwegians.

Konstantin Gorbatov launched his career by exhibiting with the Peredvizhniki, or Wanderers, a group of Russian realists who rejected academic restrictions. After the Russian Revolution he left Russia in 1922, first settling in Capri and then in Berlin. There he joined a Russian émigré art group that included Leonid Pasternak, Vadim Falileyev and Ivan Myasoyedov. In 1934 he visited Palestine and Syria. His work was deemed unneeded during the Nazi regime, which ended his career.

Karl Wilhelm Diefenbach was the son of a painter and drawing teacher in Hadamar, who gave him his first artistic lessons. He then studied at the Munich Academy of Fine Arts and was impressed by Arnold Böcklin and Franz von Stuck. His right arm was crippled by severe typhoid fever and a botched operation, so he had to learn to write and paint with his left hand. Regarded as the forefather of alternative movements, he championed naturism and pacifism. His rural commune Himmelhof near Vienna inspired his student Gustav Gräser to found the Monte Verità settlement near Ascona.

John Sartain learned line engraving and produced several plates in William Young Ottley's Early Florentine School. He began making mezzotints in 1828 and studied painting under John Varley and Henry James Richter. In 1830 he emigrated to the United States and settled in Philadelphia, where he studied with Joshua Shaw. For about ten years he painted portraits in oil and miniatures on ivory, and he also made designs for banknote vignettes and drew on wood for book illustrations. He pioneered mezzotint engraving in the United States.

Jacopo de' Barbari moved from Venice to Germany in 1500, becoming the first Italian Renaissance artist of stature to work in Northern Europe. His place and date of birth are unknown, though Albrecht Dürer described him as a Venetian. About twelve of his paintings survive, among them the first known example of trompe-l'œil since antiquity. His twenty-nine engravings and three very large woodcuts were also influential. He signed most of his engravings with a caduceus, the sign of Mercury.

Ludovico Carracci apprenticed under Prospero Fontana in Bologna and traveled to Florence, Parma and Venice before returning to his hometown. With his cousins Annibale and Agostino he worked on the fresco cycles of Jason and Medea in Palazzo Fava and Romulus and Remus in Palazzo Magnani. Annibale, who gained fame as the best of the three, went on to paint the Loves of the Gods in Rome, while Ludovico remained in Bologna. His works are characterized by a strong mood invoked by broad gestures and flickering light. He died in Bologna in 1619.

Victor Westerholm grew up in Turku as the son of a ship's master and spent much of his childhood on the island of Nagu in the Finnish Archipelago. He studied at the Finnish Art Society's Drawing School in Turku, then in Düsseldorf under Eugen Dücker, and much later at the Académie Julian in Paris. In 1891 he became director of the Turku art museum. He visited the Åland Islands almost every summer, often painting winter landscapes and sunsets at his summer home Tomtebo in Önningeby. He is especially known for founding the Önningeby artists' colony.

Kamisaka Sekka grew up in Kyoto in a samurai family, where his talents for art and design were recognized early. He allied himself with the traditional Rinpa school and is considered its last great proponent. In 1901 the Japanese government sent him to Glasgow, where he was heavily influenced by Art Nouveau. He wanted to learn which elements of Japanese art would attract the West. On returning he taught at the newly opened Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts and worked in lacquer and other media.

Jacques Bellange worked for fourteen years in Nancy as court painter to two Dukes of Lorraine and died at about forty. None of his paintings are known to survive, so his etchings and some drawings are his only securely identified works. Almost all his prints were produced in the three or four years before his death, mostly on Catholic religious subjects and in a highly individual style. Collectors have known them since shortly after his death. His place of birth is unknown, but most French sources assume the Bassigny region.

Johann Leonhard Raab was educated in public schools in Nuremberg and attended the Academy of Fine Arts there. He began as a painter but was soon attracted to engraving and began formal studies with Samuel Amsler. At first he concentrated on small plates for book publishers. In 1866, on the recommendation of Julius Thaeter, he succeeded him as Professor of Engraving at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. He retired in 1895 and opened a painting studio with three friends. His daughter Doris Raab became his pupil and exhibited at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Nikolai Triik came from a middle-class family and enrolled at the Saint Petersburg Art and Industry Academy after finishing public school, but was expelled for taking part in a student strike during the 1905 Revolution. He returned home to study at Ants Laikmaa's private art school, then went back to Saint Petersburg to take lessons from Osip Braz. He later married the daughter of a wealthy factory owner and moved to Paris, where he sampled courses at the Académie Colarossi, the Académie Julian and the École des Beaux-arts. His work displays elements of Symbolism and Expressionism.

Käthe Kollwitz was the fifth child of a Social Democrat father who became a mason and house builder, and her grandfather Julius Rupp, a Lutheran pastor expelled from the official church, greatly influenced her education and her art. Her father arranged for her to begin lessons in drawing and copying plaster casts when she was twelve. Her best-known cycles, The Weavers and The Peasant War, depict the effects of poverty and war on the working class. She was the first woman elected to the Prussian Academy of Arts.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder returned from his training and travels in Italy in 1555 to settle in Antwerp, where he worked mainly as a designer of prints for the leading publisher of the day. At the end of the 1550s he made painting his main medium, and all his famous paintings come from the following period of little more than a decade. He was known for landscapes and peasant scenes and was a pioneer in presenting both as large paintings. Landscape with the Fall of Icarus and The Hunters in the Snow have inspired artists in literature and cinema.

Hendrick Avercamp studied in Amsterdam with the Danish-born portrait painter Pieter Isaacsz, and perhaps also with David Vinckboons. In 1608 he moved to Kampen. He was mute and probably deaf and was known as de Stomme van Kampen, the mute of Kampen. He specialized in painting the Netherlands in winter, and many of his paintings feature people ice skating on frozen lakes. He sold his drawings, many tinted with watercolor, as finished pictures to be pasted into the albums of collectors.

Leopold Carl Müller, the Dresden-born son of Austrian parents, studied with Karl von Blaas and Christian Ruben at the Academy in Vienna. To support his family after his father died, he worked eight years as an illustrator for the Vienna Figaro. He visited Italy and Egypt repeatedly and made his name with scenes of popular life in Italy and Hungary. In the late 1860s a visit to Paris and the work of Eugène Fromentin turned him toward Orientalist subjects. In 1877 he became a professor at the Vienna Academy, and his pupils included Ludwig Deutsch and Pavle Paja Jovanović.

Jan Willem Pieneman first worked as a salesman while taking courses at the Amsterdam Stadstekenacademie. In 1805 he became drawing instructor at the artillery and engineering training centre in Amersfoort. His fame was established by a painting at Villa Welgelegen of the Prince of Orange at the Battle of Quatre Bras, followed by one of the Battle of Waterloo. The Duke of Wellington liked the latter and invited him to England several times to paint portraits. In 1820 he became first director of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Amsterdam, a position he held until his death.

Ike no Taiga grew up in a poor family. His father, a farmer on the outskirts of Kyoto, found work at the silver mint but died when Taiga was three. His widowed mother managed to give him good teachers in the classical Japanese and Chinese disciplines. At six he began receiving instruction in calligraphy and religious matters at the Manpuku-ji Zen temple. Together with Yosa Buson he perfected the bunjinga genre. Most of his works reflect his passion for classical Chinese culture and painting techniques, though he also incorporated modern techniques into otherwise traditional paintings.

Sebastiaen Vrancx was the son of an Antwerp merchant and apprenticed in the workshop of Adam van Noort, who also taught Rubens, Jordaens and Hendrick van Balen. It is believed he visited Italy, since he only became a master of the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke in 1600. He is mainly known for battle scenes, a genre he pioneered in Netherlandish painting. He was regularly invited to paint the staffage in compositions of fellow painters. As a member of a chamber of rhetoric he wrote comedies and poems, and he was also captain of the Antwerp civic guard.

Giovanni Lanfranco, the third son of Stefano and Cornelia Lanfranchi of Parma, was placed as a page in the household of Count Orazio Scotti. His talent for drawing led to an apprenticeship with Agostino Carracci, working alongside Sisto Badalocchio in the local Farnese palaces. When Agostino died in 1602, both young artists moved to Annibale Carracci's large Roman workshop, which was working on the Galleria Farnese ceiling. Lanfranco is considered to have contributed to the panel of Polyphemus and Galatea. He belonged to the Bolognese school, deeply influenced by Annibale's classicism.

Gerrit Berckheyde learned to paint from his older brother Job, who was eleven years his senior. During the 1650s the brothers made an extended trip along the Rhine to Germany, stopping off at Cologne and Heidelberg. They worked there for the Elector Palatine Charles I Louis and both received a golden medal, but they could not adapt to court life and returned to Haarlem, where they shared a house and studio. He was active in Haarlem, Amsterdam and The Hague and is best known today for his cityscapes.

Jules Gervais-Courtellemont emigrated with his parents to Algeria as a boy, where they started a family agricultural business that quickly failed. He stayed for twenty years and developed a passion for the pre-colonial Orient. In 1894 he converted to Islam before making a pilgrimage to Mecca, and Hachette published his book Mon Voyage a la Mecque in 1896. After experiments with monochrome photography, he adopted the Autochrome Lumière system. In 1911 he opened the Palais de l'autochromie in Paris, with an exhibition hall, studio, laboratory and lecture hall seating 250, where he projected his autochromes of the Orient.

Johann Christian Reinhart was encouraged to draw by a teacher at the gymnasium in Hof. He started to study theology like his father but turned more and more to art. He studied under Adam Friedrich Oeser in Leipzig and later under Johann Christian Klengel in Dresden, who taught him chiefly after the Dutch masters. In 1785 he struck up a friendship with Friedrich Schiller. In 1789, supported by a grant from the Margrave of Ansbach-Bayreuth, he left Dresden for Rome. With Joseph Anton Koch he is counted among the founders of German romantic classical landscape painting.

Louis Valtat grew up in Versailles in a wealthy family of ship owners, and his father, an amateur landscape painter, encouraged his interest in art. At seventeen he decided on an artistic career and applied to the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. He was accepted, and in 1887 he moved to Paris to study with Gustave Boulanger, Jules Lefebvre and later Jean-Joseph Benjamin-Constant. He then studied at the Académie Julian under Jules Dupré. Associated with the Fauves, who first exhibited together in 1905 at the Salon d'Automne, he is noted as a figure in the transition from Monet to Matisse.

Hans Rottenhammer studied in Munich under Hans Donauer the Elder until 1588. He was in Rome in the early 1590s and settled in Venice in the mid-1590s, staying until 1606 before returning to Germany and settling in Augsburg. In Venice he gained a reputation for small, highly finished cabinet paintings on copper of religious and mythological subjects, combining German and Italian elements of style. He combined the landscape tradition of the North with the compositional and figure styles of Tintoretto and Veronese. He died in Augsburg, apparently in poverty.

Randolph Caldecott was the third child of a tailor-turned-accountant in Chester and drew and modelled animals from early childhood. He illustrated novels and accounts of foreign travel, made humorous drawings of hunting and fashionable life, and exhibited sculptures and paintings at the Royal Academy. He also sketched the Houses of Parliament inside and out. He is most remembered for his illustrations of children's books, which transformed the style of book illustration. His brother Alfred became an eminent philosopher.

Hermann Ottomar Herzog entered the Düsseldorf Academy at seventeen, studying with Schirmer and Rudolph Wiegmann and taking private lessons with Andreas Achenbach and Hans Gude. After traveling and painting in Norway he achieved early commercial success, with patrons including royalty and nobility throughout Europe. In 1871 he immigrated to the United States and traveled extensively, including California in 1873 and Mexico. He is associated with the Düsseldorf School and the Hudson River School of painting.

John Glover achieved fame as a painter of Italianate romantic landscapes of Britain and Southern Europe, and he became known in England and France as the English Claude. The Countess of Harrington helped establish his practice as an art instructor. He came from a farming family in Leicestershire. In later life he migrated to Van Diemen's Land and became a pastoralist in the early colonial period. He has been dubbed the father of Australian landscape painting.

Carl Peter Burnitz was orphaned at nine and placed in the care of his uncle, the architect Rudolf Burnitz. He studied law at Berlin and Heidelberg and received his doctorate of law in 1847, then toured Italy. Back in Frankfurt he briefly practiced law but, dissatisfied and inspired by what he had seen, took another trip in 1852 to Algiers and Madrid. In Madrid the painter Fritz Bamberger suggested he study art in Paris, where Karl Bodmer introduced him to the Barbizon School. He studied with Emile Lambinet and returned to Frankfurt in 1857, where he befriended Anton Burger.

Pieter de Hooch was the eldest of five children of a bricklayer and a midwife in Rotterdam, in a working-class home. Little is known about his early life, and the archives suggest he worked in Rotterdam and Delft. He belonged to the Delft Guild of Saint Luke like his contemporary Jan Vermeer, whose themes and style his work shares. He is known for genre works of quiet domestic scenes with an open doorway. He was last documented in 1679, and his son Pieter died in 1684, a date often wrongly given for the father.

Paul Désiré Trouillebert studied under Ernest Hébert and Charles Jalabert. He made his debut at the Salon of 1865 at thirty-six and exhibited at least one portrait there for several years. His interests then shifted toward landscape painting. More than a thousand of his works are included in the catalogue raisonné of his paintings, published in 2004. Most are landscapes, though many portraits and orientalist genre pictures appear as well. His works are in museums including the Musée d'Orsay, the Hermitage Museum and the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Johann Heinrich Tischbein was the son of a baker, five of whose eight children became painters, and he studied wallpaper painting and later oil painting with Johann Georg von Freese, then worked for small princely courts. Count Johann Philipp von Stadion sponsored him in 1743 to study with Carle van Loo in Paris. In 1749 he studied with Giovanni Battista Piazzetta in Venice. A year in Rome followed. In 1753 he became court painter to the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel. His work consisted primarily of portraits of the nobility, mythological scenes and historical paintings.
